newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand accepts central bank chief's resignation.
newsitem.headline: Thailand accepts central bank chief's resignation.

text.p: Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said on Tuesday he had accepted the resignation of Bank of Thailand Governor Rerngchai Marakanond.
"We will discuss his replacement at the cabinet meeting today," he told reporters before attending a weekly cabinet meeting being held this week in this northwestern border town.
Rerngchai submitted his resignation late on Monday and was not available for comment.
His resignation comes on the heels of a government decision to accept IMF advice on how to fix the Thai economy, which is going through its worst slump in more than a decade.
Thailand is also studying whether or not to seek a standby credit line from the world body to help the country overcome current tight liquidity problems.
Government sources and analysts said the front-runner to replace Rerngchai was his deputy, Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi.

The governor, who took office last July, had been criticised after the authorities decided to put the baht into a managed float on July 2. The baht has since declined by more than 20 percent, hurting business.
Rerngchai had also been under pressure over his handling of troubles in the financial sector, which has been hit by a liquidity crunch and overexposure to the depressed property sector.
The central bank has also come under fire for keeping interest rates high in defence of the embattled baht.
There had been rumours in recent weeks in the market that the governor was planning to resign, but such speculation has previously been quashed by him and the authorities.

On Monday, Rerngchai, in his last official statement before quitting, told reporters that Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh and Thanong had agreed in principle as far back as July 22 to take loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
His remarks came as the finance minister took pains to say that any borrowing from the IMF was still being studied and a decision would only be made after that.
Politicians fear IMF assistance might come with unpopular strings attached.
Thailand confirmed on Monday that it was in talks with the IMF on advice to resuscitate its battered economy.

Last Friday, Rerngchai also took the unusual step of defending his bank's policy to float the baht, saying the decision was made through established procedure and with the knowledge of Thanong and the finance ministry's permanent secretary.
He said the decision to float the baht was not exclusively his, saying it was an agreement reached by senior central bank and finance ministry officials responsible for such policy.
"The governor has never issued instructions or taken decisions contrary to proposals made by senior central bank officials. Any such accusations are therefore groundless," he said.

"Some reports said the prime minister ordered the central bank governor to change the exchange rate system. But under legal and established procedure..., which can be verified, it is the governor who would make such a proposal to the finance minister for his approval before it is forwarded to the prime minister," he said.
